books.section: Topic 4.11 An Age of Reform, D. The Women's Rights Movement

primary_sources: Sarah Grimké, Letters on the Equality of the Sexes, 1838

stimulus.text: "But I ask no favors for my sex. I surrender not our claim to equality. All I ask of our brethren is, that they will take their feet from off our necks, and permit us to stand upright on that ground which God designed us to occupy." — Sarah Grimké, Letters on the Equality of the Sexes, 1838
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim public-domain quotation from Sarah Grimké, Letters on the Equality of the Sexes (Boston: Isaac Knapp, 1838), Letter II, written July 1837. Wording checked against the Project Gutenberg edition. Note: the passage is Sarah Grimké's, not her sister Angelina's.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain quotation from Sarah Grimké, Letters (1838)

options.text: women be given favors and protection by men
options.misconception: Grimké says plainly, 'I ask no favors for my sex.'

options.text: women withdraw from public life and speaking
options.misconception: Grimké writes and speaks in public; she demands a public voice, not silence.

options.text: men stop standing in the way of women's equality
women be given the vote immediately at Seneca Falls
options.misconception: The vote comes later; this letter demands equality in general, not the ballot in particular.

rationales.A: Grimké opens with 'I ask no favors for my sex.' Favors are exactly what she refuses.
rationales.B: Grimké's letters were published in newspapers and read across the country. She claims public life for women, not withdrawal from it.
rationales.C: Grimké asks only that men take their feet from off women's necks and let women stand upright. Her demand is that men stop blocking equality.
rationales.D: The letter claims equality, not the ballot box in particular. The vote becomes the movement's central demand at Seneca Falls, ten years later.
rationales.general:
1. Read the first sentence. Grimké asks no favors and surrenders no claim to equality.
2. Read the image. Men stand with their feet on women's necks, holding them down.
3. Name the demand. She asks men to step off, not to hand women a gift.
Background: Sarah Grimké wrote these letters in 1837 after ministers condemned women speaking in public.
Remember: 'take your feet off our necks' is a demand to stop blocking, not a plea for a favor — read the verb.
